chapter: Lucky Roberts, Armstrong and the big-band rivalries
title: Bix Beiderbecke's playing within his range
summary: Butler hung out with Bix, who drank gin, and praises him for playing only what he knew and resolving every note, a lesson he links to Slossberg's advice.

story.theme_name: Remembering the early trumpeters and their styles
story.community_name: Bix Beiderbecke: hearing, copying and remembering him

blocks.x: Now also Beiderbecke, you knew him, too, right?

Oh, yeah, knew Bix Beiderbecke. We hung around together. We used to go to races. And he loved to drink gin, and at that time I had my beer, the only good thing was beer. And he'd just / And then he'd have to go to work, he'd send him to work in a taxi somewhere. We'd have to just go direct to work. He didn't take care of his body.
What did you think of him as a trumpet player?

Well, he knew the trumpet. He wasn't a robust-built fellow. But what he was trying to get those high notes -- and this is what was destruction of a lot of trumpeters, they were trying to reach Louis Armstrong and they were destroying themselves. Because Bix Beiderbecke, as long as he's played, his range, I think, was B natural. And as long as he played this within range, he never made no -- (inaudible) difficult things. And what he played was good. It made sense and it was him, and it swung. He could swing. In his way.
But he wasn't sounding bad, then. He was sounding good.
I know you told me once in the bar that the thing that impressed most of the guys about him was he could resolve any note that he played.

That's what I'm trying to say. What he played was right. And see, when the light comes on, well, there's nothing you can say about it; it's crystal; what he played was right. Because you see, a lot of times you'd be swinging and a couple long notes would be in there, but he'd find a way to make them right. He'd bend over and everything, and the notes would come out right. Because he was taking chances. But this man knew, so he didn't have to take chances. You see the difference?
Sonny Greer told me that you couldn't get him on the bandstand with Bubber Miley (inaudible).
Well, you see, Bubber Miley would get up

there and confound him because you'd hear something and you said, well, what is he doing up there, and you'd forget what you were doing. Because you'd be hearing some stuff and you'd forget what you were doing. So you're not going to take no chances. You're going to play just what you could execute. You're not going out and try -- you see what I mean?

And that is what Slossberg told me. He says, play what you know and yourself. And if some other man is playing, don't be awed at what he is doing because probably if you play what you know, he'll be looking up at you.
